topic.title: Words Functioning as Different Parts of Speech

lesson.lesson_summary: Learn how the same English word can do different grammatical jobs in different sentences. Discover how to identify a word's part of speech by looking at how it is used, rather than memorising only its meaning.

learning_objectives.description: Understand that the same word can belong to different parts of speech depending on its use in a sentence.
success_criteria: Explain why a word does not always have one fixed grammatical role.
Recognise that a word's function depends on its use in a sentence.

learning_objectives.description: Identify words functioning as nouns and verbs in different sentences.
success_criteria: Identify a word used as a noun.
Identify the same word used as a verb.
Explain the difference using sentence context.

learning_objectives.description: Identify words functioning as different parts of speech beyond nouns and verbs.
success_criteria: Recognise words used as adjectives and verbs.
Recognise words used as nouns and adjectives.
Recognise words used as adjectives and adverbs.

learning_objectives.description: Recognise words that can function as prepositions, conjunctions and adverbs.
success_criteria: Identify the grammatical role of a word in different sentence structures.
Distinguish between different uses of the same word.

learning_objectives.description: Determine the part of speech of a word by examining its function in a complete sentence.
success_criteria: Use surrounding words to identify grammatical function.
Classify a word correctly in an unfamiliar sentence.
Avoid identifying parts of speech from word meaning alone.

learning_objectives.description: Correct common mistakes when identifying words with multiple grammatical functions.
success_criteria: Explain why a word has a particular grammatical function.
Correctly classify the same word across different sentences.

learning_dimensions.dimension: Other Parts of Speech and Their Functions

pages.title: One Word, Two Jobs!

content.text: Did you know that one English word can do different jobs? A word can be a noun in one sentence and a verb in another!

examples.explanation: Book names something. It is a noun.
Book tells us what action to do. It is a verb.

pages.key_takeaway: One word can have different grammatical jobs.

pages.title: What Is a Word's Job?

content.text: Every word has a job in a sentence. This job is called its grammatical function or part of speech.

examples.explanation: Rita is a noun. It names a person.
Runs is a verb. It tells us what Rita does.

pages.key_takeaway: A part of speech tells us what job a word does.

content.text: Never decide a word's part of speech by looking at the word alone. Look at the complete sentence to understand its job.

items.label: The word alone
items.description: Does not always tell us its grammatical function.

comparison_points: A word's grammatical role depends on how it is used.
content.conclusion: Always examine the sentence before identifying a part of speech.

pages.title: A Noun Can Become a Verb

content.text: Some words can name things and also describe actions. Their grammatical jobs change with the sentence.

examples.explanation: Here, play is a noun. It names an activity.
Here, play is a verb. It tells us what the children do.

content.title: Remember
content.text: A noun names something. A verb tells us what happens or what someone does.

pages.key_takeaway: Play can be a noun or a verb.

pages.title: More Noun and Verb Examples

content.text: Look at these words. Each one can name something or describe an action.

comparison_points: The same word form can name something or describe an action.
content.conclusion: Check whether the word names something or expresses an action.

pages.key_takeaway: Water and answer can also change their jobs.

pages.title: An Adjective Can Become a Noun

content.text: Some words describe people or things. The same words can sometimes name a group or a person.

examples.explanation: Poor is used as a noun. It refers to people who are poor.
Poor is an adjective. It describes the man.

content.title: A Useful Point
content.text: When an adjective refers to a whole group of people, it can function as a noun. For example, the rich, the young and the elderly.

pages.key_takeaway: The same describing word can also name a group.

pages.title: An Adjective Can Become a Verb

content.text: Some words describe a quality. They can also describe an action that changes something.

examples.explanation: Clean describes the room. It is an adjective.
Clean tells us what action to do. It is a verb.
Dry describes the floor. It is an adjective.
Dry tells us to remove the water. It is a verb.

pages.key_takeaway: Clean and dry can be adjectives or verbs.

pages.title: An Adjective Can Become an Adverb

content.text: Some words can describe a noun in one sentence and describe an action in another.

examples.explanation: Fast describes the runner. It is an adjective.
Fast describes how she runs. It is an adverb.

content.title: Important
content.text: Not every adverb ends in -ly. Fast is an adverb in the second sentence.

pages.key_takeaway: Fast can be an adjective or an adverb.

pages.title: More Adjective and Adverb Examples

content.text: Some words can describe a noun or tell us how an action happens. Notice the difference.

comparison_points: An adverb can describe a verb or an action.
content.conclusion: The word's job changes according to what it describes.

pages.key_takeaway: Hard and early can have different grammatical functions.

pages.title: A Word Can Be a Preposition

content.text: Some words can show a relationship between things. The same words may have other jobs in different sentences.

examples.sentence: The cat is inside the box.
examples.explanation: Inside is a preposition. It shows where the cat is in relation to the box.
Inside is an adverb. It tells us where the cat is, without an object after it.

content.title: Look Carefully
content.text: A preposition normally has an object. An adverb does not take an object in this use.

pages.key_takeaway: Inside can be a preposition or an adverb.

pages.title: A Word Can Be a Conjunction

content.text: Some words connect ideas or parts of sentences. They may also have other grammatical jobs.

items.label: Before — Preposition
items.description: Comes before a noun or noun phrase.

items.label: Before — Conjunction
items.description: Connects a dependent clause to another clause.
items.example: I arrived before the show started.

items.label: Before — Adverb
items.description: Refers to an earlier time without an object or following clause.

comparison_points: An adverb can stand without either.
content.conclusion: The grammatical structure after before helps identify its job.

pages.key_takeaway: Before can be a preposition, conjunction or adverb.

pages.title: How Can You Find the Job?

content.text: Ask a simple question about the word. Does it name something, describe something, show an action or connect ideas?

items: Noun: Does it name someone or something?
Verb: Does it express an action or state?
Adjective: Does it describe a noun?
Adverb: Does it describe a verb, adjective or another adverb?
Preposition: Does it show a relationship with an object?
Conjunction: Does it connect words, phrases or clauses?

pages.key_takeaway: Ask what job the word is doing.

pages.title: Same Word, Different Sentences

content.text: Let's examine the word light. It can do several different jobs.

comparison_points: The word light has different grammatical functions in these sentences.
content.conclusion: A single word form can perform several grammatical jobs.

pages.key_takeaway: Light can be a noun, adjective or verb.

pages.title: Try Identifying the Job

content.text: Read each sentence carefully. Look at the highlighted word and decide what job it performs.

examples.explanation: Watch is a verb. It describes what the children do.
Watch is a noun. It names an object.

pages.key_takeaway: Always use the complete sentence as your clue.

pages.title: Common Mistake: Fixed Labels

content.text: A common mistake is thinking that a word always belongs to the same part of speech.

mistake.correct: Book can be a noun or a verb.
mistake.reason: In 'I bought a book', it names something. In 'Book a ticket', it expresses an action.

pages.key_takeaway: Never give a word one permanent part-of-speech label.

pages.title: Meaning Is Not Enough

content.text: A word's meaning alone does not decide its part of speech. Its grammatical role in the sentence is what matters.

mistake.correct: Fast can be an adjective or an adverb.
mistake.reason: In 'a fast car', fast describes a noun. In 'drive fast', it describes the action.

pages.key_takeaway: Check the word's grammatical function, not just its meaning.

pages.title: Test Your Understanding

content.text: You have learned that words can change their grammatical jobs. Try identifying their functions in these sentences.

pages.key_takeaway: Find the job before choosing the part of speech.

pages.title: Remember These Rules

content.text: The same word can perform different grammatical jobs in different sentences. Its function depends on how it is used.

items: A word does not always have one fixed part of speech.
Nouns can also function as verbs.
Adjectives can also function as nouns or verbs.
Some adjectives can also function as adverbs.
Some words can function as prepositions, conjunctions or adverbs.

pages.key_takeaway: One word. Different jobs. The sentence tells you which one.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is the word watch in this sentence: 'I bought a new watch'?
question_bank.explanation: Watch names an object in this sentence. Therefore, it is a noun.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is fast in this sentence: 'The car moves fast'?
question_bank.explanation: Fast tells us how the car moves. It describes the action and functions as an adverb.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is before in this sentence: 'I arrived before the bell rang'?
question_bank.explanation: Before introduces the clause 'the bell rang' and connects it to the main clause. Therefore, it functions as a conjunction.

question_bank.prompt: The word book can function as both a noun and a verb.
question_bank.explanation: Book is a noun in 'I read a book' and a verb in 'Book a room'.

question_bank.prompt: What decides the part of speech of a word?

options.text: The number of letters in the word
Its grammatical function in the sentence

question_bank.explanation: A word's grammatical function in its sentence determines its part of speech.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is answer in this sentence: 'Please answer my question'?
question_bank.explanation: Answer tells us what action someone should perform. It is a verb.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is clean in this sentence: 'Please clean your shoes'?
question_bank.explanation: Clean expresses the action of making the shoes free from dirt. It is a verb.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is poor in this sentence: 'The poor need support'?
question_bank.explanation: The poor refers to people who are poor. The word poor functions as a noun in this expression.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is inside in this sentence: 'The children are inside the classroom'?
question_bank.explanation: Inside shows the relationship between the children and the classroom. The noun phrase 'the classroom' is its object.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is before in this sentence: 'I have met her before'?
question_bank.explanation: Before refers to an earlier time. It does not introduce an object or a clause, so it functions as an adverb.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is light in this sentence: 'Light the candle'?
question_bank.explanation: Light tells someone to perform an action. It is an imperative verb.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is hard in this sentence: 'She works hard'?
question_bank.explanation: Hard describes how she works. It functions as an adverb.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is play in this sentence: 'The children play outside'?
question_bank.explanation: Play tells us what the children do. It functions as a verb.

options.text: Every word has only one part of speech.
A word's part of speech depends on its function in the sentence.
Only nouns can change their grammatical jobs.
A word's spelling always tells us its part of speech.

question_bank.explanation: The same word form can perform different grammatical functions in different sentences.

question_bank.prompt: Correct the grammatical classification in this statement: 'In the sentence She runs fast, fast is an adjective.'
question_bank.original_sentence: In the sentence She runs fast, fast is an adjective.
question_bank.corrected_sentence: In the sentence She runs fast, fast is an adverb.
question_bank.explanation: Fast describes how she runs. It modifies the verb runs, so it functions as an adverb.

final_assessment.title: One Word, Different Jobs — Final Check

cross_references.reason: Some words acquire an additional grammatical function without changing their spelling, such as book used as a noun or verb. The linguistic process of forming a new word through conversion is related but requires a separate lesson.
This lesson focuses on the same word form performing different grammatical functions, not changes such as play, plays and played.
Some verb forms can perform noun-like or adjective-like functions. These involve additional grammatical structures and require separate lessons.
This lesson demonstrates selected words with multiple grammatical functions. A complete study of all parts of speech and their classifications belongs to the broader Parts of Speech lesson.

issues_found: The complete Learn Lesson JSON Schema v2.0 definition was not included in the supplied prompt file. Structural compliance with the actual JSON Schema cannot therefore be independently certified.
The lesson introduces selected examples of words functioning as different parts of speech. It is not an exhaustive dictionary of all English words that can perform multiple grammatical functions.

The expression 'the poor' is treated as a noun phrase with poor functioning substantivally. Some grammar frameworks classify this as an adjective used substantively rather than a conventional noun. The distinction may be introduced in an advanced lesson.
The example 'The children play is starting' was avoided in favour of clearer examples elsewhere; the noun play is illustrated through its use in 'The play was funny' in the comparison section.
